title: Unit 4: Contextual Applications of Differentiation

topics.name: Rates of change in context and motion
covers: Identifying relevant mathematical information in verbal representations of real-world problems involving rates of change
Applying understandings of differentiation to problems involving motion
Generalizing understandings of motion problems to other situations involving rates of change

guide.title: Contextual applications of differentiation: review guide
guide.intro: Derivatives describe real rates. This unit interprets them in context and in motion, links rates that change together, approximates values with tangent lines, and uses L'Hospital's rule for indeterminate limits.

sections.title: Rates of change in context and motion
body: A derivative's units are output units per input unit. If W(t) is gallons and t is hours, W′(3) = −12 means that at t = 3 hours the amount is decreasing at 12 gallons per hour.
For motion, velocity v(t) = s′(t), acceleration a(t) = v′(t), and speed is |v(t)|. The particle is at rest where v = 0 and changes direction where v changes sign.
points: Speeding up when v and a have the same sign; slowing down when they have opposite signs.
Always state units and the time in an interpretation.
The same reasoning applies to any quantity's rate of change.

sections.title: Related rates
body: When quantities that change together are linked by an equation, differentiate the equation with respect to time to link their rates. Substitute the specific values only after differentiating.
Steps: draw and label the situation, write an equation relating the quantities, differentiate implicitly in t, then substitute and solve.
points: Use similar triangles to remove an extra variable (as in a cone).
Signs matter: a decreasing quantity has a negative rate.
Substituting numbers first freezes the variables and gives a rate of 0.

sections.title: Local linearity and L'Hospital's rule
body: Near x = a, a differentiable function is close to its tangent line: f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a). The approximation is an overestimate when f is concave down and an underestimate when f is concave up.
L'Hospital's rule: if lim f(x)/g(x) gives 0/0 or ∞/∞, then it equals lim f′(x)/g′(x) when that limit exists. Differentiate the top and bottom separately; you may need to apply it more than once.
points: Check the form first; L'Hospital's rule doesn't apply to forms like 1/0.
Logarithms grow more slowly than any positive power of x.
Never use the quotient rule inside L'Hospital's rule.

example.prompt: A spherical balloon's radius grows at 0.5 cm/s. How fast is its volume growing when r = 6 cm?

misconceptions: Slowing down depends on whether velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.
Substituting first turns changing quantities into constants, whose rates are 0.
Differentiate the numerator and denominator separately.
“A tangent-line estimate is always too high.”
It overestimates only where the function is concave down.

questions.prompt: W(t) is the number of gallons of water in a tank t hours after noon. What does W′(3) = −12 mean?
choices: The tank loses 12 gallons every 3 hours
At 3 p.m., the tank holds 12 gallons less than at noon
At 3 p.m., the amount of water is decreasing at 12 gallons per hour
At 3 p.m., the tank holds −12 gallons
questions.explanation: W′(3) is the instantaneous rate of change at t = 3 (3 p.m.), in gallons per hour; the negative sign means the amount is decreasing.
choiceExplanations: W′(3) is the rate at one instant, not an average over 3 hours.
That describes the total change W(3) − W(0), not the rate at 3 p.m.
W′(3) is a rate, not the amount of water.

questions.prompt: A particle moves along a line with position s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t for t ≥ 0. At what times is it at rest?
questions.explanation: v(t) = s′(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t − 1)(t − 3), which is 0 at t = 1 and t = 3.
choiceExplanations: t = 2 is where the acceleration is 0.
At t = 0 the velocity is 9, so the particle is moving.
t = 0 and t = 3 are where the position is 0, not where the velocity is 0.

questions.prompt: A particle's velocity is v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 for t ≥ 0. On which intervals is it speeding up?
questions.explanation: v(t) = (t − 1)(t − 3) and a(t) = 2t − 4. Speeding up needs v and a to have the same sign: on (1, 2) both are negative, and for t > 3 both are positive.
choiceExplanations: On (2, 3) the signs differ, so the particle slows down there.
For 2 < t < 3, v < 0 but a > 0, so the particle is slowing down there.
On (0, 1), v > 0 but a < 0, so it is slowing down.

questions.prompt: A circle's radius increases at 2 cm/s. How fast is its area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?
questions.explanation: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt = 2π(5)(2) = 20π cm²/s.
choiceExplanations: 25π is the area at r = 5, not its rate of change.
10π leaves out the factor dr/dt = 2.
4π uses r = 1 instead of r = 5.

questions.prompt: A 10 ft ladder leans against a wall. Its bottom slides away from the wall at 2 ft/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is 6 ft from the wall?
questions.explanation: x² + y² = 100, so 2x·dx/dt + 2y·dy/dt = 0. When x = 6, y = 8, and dy/dt = −(6)(2)/8 = −1.5: the top slides down at 1.5 ft/s.
choiceExplanations: The top's speed differs from the bottom's because x and y change by different amounts.
2.7 ft/s uses the ratio y/x = 8/6 instead of x/y.
1.2 ft/s uses x/10 instead of x/y.

questions.prompt: Water flows at 3 m³/min into a cone-shaped tank with its vertex at the bottom. The tank's radius is always half its height. How fast is the water level rising when the water is 2 m deep?
questions.explanation: With r = h/2, V = (1/3)π(h/2)²h = πh³/12. Then dV/dt = (πh²/4) dh/dt. At h = 2: 3 = π · dh/dt, so dh/dt = 3/π ≈ 0.95 m/min.
choiceExplanations: 12/π leaves out the h² = 4 factor, as if h were 1.
1/π uses the cylinder volume πr²h, leaving out the cone's factor 1/3.
3/(4π) uses r = h instead of r = h/2.

questions.prompt: Using the tangent line to f(x) = √x at x = 16, what is the approximate value of √16.2?
choiceExplanations: 4.0125 uses a slope of 1/16.
4.2 assumes the slope is 1.
4.05 uses a slope of 1/4 instead of 1/8.

questions.explanation: This is 0/0, so apply L'Hospital's rule: (eˣ − 1)/(2x), still 0/0. Again: eˣ/2 → 1/2.
choiceExplanations: The limit exists; L'Hospital's rule twice gives 1/2.
1 stops after the first application and guesses; the second application gives 1/2.
Substituting gives 0/0, which is indeterminate, not 0.

questions.explanation: This is ∞/∞. L'Hospital: (1/x)/(1/(2√x)) = 2√x/x = 2/√x → 0. Logarithms grow more slowly than any positive power of x.
choiceExplanations: The ratio isn't 1; √x eventually dwarfs ln x.
Both grow without bound, but √x grows much faster than ln x.
2 comes from stopping at 2√x/x without simplifying its limit.
